payload.name: SearchActivityFactsAcrossPredicates
payload.description: When answering what activities/hobbies a person pursues (with or without an excluded topic), supplement structured predicate='activity' searches with semantic/free-text searches for concrete activity terms across memory kinds.
content: When a question asks what activities or hobbies a person pursues (including 'besides', 'apart from', or 'other than' an excluded topic), do not rely only on structured queries with predicate='activity'; activity facts are often embedded in event/preference/state memories with other predicates or in free-text descriptions.

Run at least one hybrid or semantic/free-text search combining the person's name with concrete activity vocabulary (e.g., running, biking, art, gardening, surfing) and without requiring the words 'activity' or 'hobby' to appear.

Before answering, if the retrieved set is missing concrete activities, widen memory_kinds beyond 'event' to include 'preference', 'profile', and 'state', and re-search each concrete activity name that appears anywhere in the session or evidence.

candidates.solves: When generic 'activities' searches miss concrete activities because facts are stored under non-activity predicates (e.g., 'discovered surfing', 'ran a gardening class'), the answer becomes incomplete. This rule supplements structured predicate='activity' queries with semantic/free-text searches for concrete activity terms and checks all memory kinds. Applies to future activity/hobby questions, including 'besides X' variants.

payload.name: SearchValueTermsForAttributeQuestions
payload.description: When a question asks for a concrete attribute value of a person's possessions or works (e.g., dog breeds, car make, music genre) and a search using only the category noun returns generic memories, run additional searches using likely value terms before answering.
content: When a question asks for the value of an attribute (breed, type, make, model, genre, cuisine), do not stop after a single search that repeats only the attribute noun; the supporting memory may express the value directly, e.g., 'Lab mix' or 'Chihuahua mix', without the noun.

Run at least one additional hybrid or keyword search using concrete value terms and synonyms (for dog breeds: 'Lab', 'Chihuahua', 'mix', 'mongrel'; for other attributes: likely brand/type/style words), and inspect low-scoring results that contain these values.

Before answering from a generic memory or saying no information, check for a more specific memory about the same subject (e.g., one listing individual pets and their breeds), and inspect its versions if the current version lacks detail.

candidates.solves: The first search for 'breeds of Audrey's dogs' returned only generic dog-care memories because the supporting memory stated 'Lab mixes' and 'Chihuahua mixes' without the word 'breeds'. The reusable mechanism is that attribute questions are answered by concrete value terms, not only the category noun; this rule applies to any future question asking about breeds, types, makes, models, genres, or cuisines where evidence may use examples instead of the umbrella term.

payload.name: EnumerateConcreteActivityTypesForCategoryQueries
payload.description: When a question asks what kinds/types of activities a person participates in within a domain (e.g., professional, academic, volunteer, creative), enumerate and search for concrete activity types like conference, workshop, internship, course, or presentation before answering.
content: When the question asks about types/kinds of activities in a domain, do not search only with the abstract category phrase. Generate a list of concrete activity types common to that domain and run at least one search per type using participation phrasing (e.g., '[subject] presented at', '[subject] attends', '[subject] interned at').

Before finalizing, verify the answer covers every enumerated activity type that has supporting evidence. If initial results lack some types, search for them explicitly, because memories often store the concrete activity (e.g., 'presented at a virtual conference') without the category label.

candidates.solves: Open-ended questions asking what kinds of activities someone participates in are answered after searching only the abstract category phrase, so memories naming concrete instances (e.g., 'presented at a virtual conference') are missed. This skill forces explicit enumeration and search for common concrete activity types in the domain before sufficiency is judged. Applies to any activity-type domain; not needed when the user already names a specific activity.

payload.name: Count items despite shared person names
payload.description: Use when counting how many of an item a person owns and a retrieved memory contains a name that also appears as a person.
content: When counting owned items and a name in the retrieved memory also refers to a person, do not exclude that name from the item count solely because of the other role.
Use context to identify item-role occurrences: phrases like 'adopted [name]', 'owns [name]', 'take [name1] and [name2] to the park', or a list of the person's pets/items.
If the name is used in an item context in any memory, count it as a separate owned item even if another memory uses the same name for a person.

candidates.solves: The agent undercounted owned items because a name that also referred to a person was excluded from the item count, even though the same memory listed that name among the owned pets. This rule abstracts the ambiguous shared-name mechanism and applies to any owned-item count where a person and an item share a name, preventing similar undercounting.

payload.name: Include event memories for commonality queries
payload.description: When a question asks what two or more entities share or have in common, include event and plan memories in retrieval; do not restrict memory_kinds to profile or preference.
content: For intersection queries asking what two or more entities have in common, set memory_kinds to include 'event' (and 'plan' or 'state' when relevant) in addition to 'profile' and 'preference'; shared circumstances such as job changes, business launches, or life milestones are typically stored as event or plan memories.

If an initial commonality search returns only one entity's preferences or profiles, run separate per-entity searches without the restrictive memory_kinds filter and examine event memories before concluding no commonality.

candidates.solves: The agent answered a two-person commonality question using only profile/preference memories, missing shared life events such as job loss and starting a business. The reusable failure is narrowing memory_kinds for intersection queries; commonalities are often episodic. Future multi-entity 'have in common' questions should broaden retrieval to event and plan memories, regardless of the people or topics involved.

payload.name: Pre-milestone problems from active-search memories
payload.description: When a question asks about problems or difficulties someone faced before a milestone (adoption, move, purchase, start), search for their active search/requirements/constraints rather than only literal problem words.
content: When a question asks what problems, difficulties, or challenges a person faced before a milestone event, run an additional search using concrete active-search and requirement phrases such as 'looking for', 'searching for', 'seeking', 'needed', 'wanted', 'finding', plus likely domain criteria, instead of only searching 'problems/issues/challenges'.

Treat memories that describe the person's active search or explicit constraints before the event (e.g., suitability for their living situation, location near desired amenities) as evidence of pre-milestone problems, even if the word problem does not appear.

candidates.solves: The failure was answering 'no information' after querying only literal problem words, while the supporting memory described the person's active search requirements before a milestone. Pre-milestone obstacles are often stored as active-search or constraint statements, not as negative labels. Future questions about problems/difficulties before an event should also retrieve concrete search/requirement vocabulary and treat it as evidence.

payload.name: Expand artifact keywords for method-of-activity questions
payload.description: When a question asks how a person remembers, records, organizes, or otherwise manages something, and initial retrieval returns only generic memories, rerun with concrete artifact nouns (board, notebook, photo, album) and inspect returned event memories.
content: If a question asks what a person does to remember, record, track, or organize something, do not answer from a single search; run additional hybrid/keyword searches pairing the person's name with concrete artifact nouns that could embody the method (e.g., notebook, journal, photo, board, album, calendar).
Inspect event memories returned by these artifact-focused searches even when they do not explicitly mention the queried activity, because the artifact often indicates the method.

candidates.solves: The failure occurred because retrieval only used 'remember'/'happy memories' and missed an event memory about a cork board that concretely represents the method. Existing skills broaden memory_kinds but do not instruct query expansion with artifact nouns. The rule applies to future 'how does X do Y' questions (remembering, recording, organizing) where evidence may be stored as event memories about physical objects; it does not apply when the method is already explicit in initial retrieval.

payload.name: Concrete re-search for abstract activity questions
payload.description: When a question asks when or how someone did something described with abstract/functional wording (e.g., 'fun indoor area') and the first search returns no close match, use concrete object and action synonyms in additional searches before concluding the answer is unavailable.
content: If a question asks about an activity using abstract or evaluative wording (e.g., 'made a fun indoor area', 'rewarding experience') and the first retrieval does not surface a memory with a clear match, do not answer 'no information' yet. Run additional hybrid/keyword searches built from concrete nouns and verbs the stored memory is likely to use (e.g., for indoor area: bed, toys, pads, crate, playpen; for making: set up, prepare, create, build).
Include structured searches on the subject entity and relevant predicates (event, preparation, plan) to catch memories whose wording differs from the question but which describe the same activity.

When the question asks for a time, use the world_start of the most concrete matching memory as the answer basis if no other memory is more precise; do not require the memory to use the question's exact wording.

candidates.solves: The search failed because the question's functional wording ('fun indoor area') did not lexically overlap with the stored memory's concrete wording ('safe space with bed, toys, puppy pads'), and the agent stopped after one search. This skill teaches the agent to bridge abstract-to-concrete vocabulary with additional synonym and structured searches before concluding evidence is missing. It applies to any access question that describes an event/activity with evaluative or functional language instead of the concrete terms in memory.

payload.name: Attribute-specific retrieval for role and position questions
payload.description: When a question asks for a specific attribute such as position, role, team, or title in connection with an action like signing or joining, use this to avoid answering from unrelated activity memories.
content: If a question asks for a specific attribute (e.g., position, role, team, title) tied to an action (e.g., signed with, joined, hired, appointed), run a targeted search that includes the subject, the action verb, and the attribute term (e.g., 'John signed position'), not just a paraphrase of the whole question.

If initial results contain memories about related activities (e.g., playing, mentoring) but none explicitly state the requested attribute, do not answer from those; search plan and event memories with the attribute term and concrete value candidates (e.g., known team names, position names) before finalizing.
Before answering an attribute question, verify that the selected evidence memory explicitly states the requested attribute; if it does not, treat the evidence as insufficient and continue searching.

candidates.solves: When asking for a specific attribute (position, role, team) tied to an action like signing or joining, retrieval can return related activity memories that lack that attribute, and the agent may answer from unrelated evidence. This skill applies to role, position, or affiliation questions where the correct fact is stored; it does not cover general activity or current-status questions.

payload.name: Search event memories for monetized passions
payload.description: When a question asks what someone loves and can make money from (earn, monetize, income, prize), also search event memories with concrete earning/competition terms before answering.
content: When a question asks what a person loves or enjoys and can make money from (e.g., monetize, earn, income, prize), do not restrict memory kinds to preference/state; run an additional search over memory_kind=event using concrete terms such as 'tournament', 'competition', 'won', 'prize', 'earned', 'paid', 'income' for that person.

If an event memory describes a win or a paid activity connected to a passion, treat it as direct evidence even when the question is phrased in terms of likes or loves; inspect the newest version of each returned memory before answering.
Do not answer from preference restatements of behavior alone when event memories about earnings may exist; run the event-kind search before concluding evidence is insufficient.

candidates.solves: Questions pairing enjoyment with monetization were answered only from preference/state memories although the decisive evidence was an enriched event memory of winning and earning. The mechanism is restricting retrieval to subjective kinds and omitting income/competition terms. Future questions joining love and money should include event-kind searches with won, prize, earned, paid, tournament; not enjoyment-only questions.

payload.name: Breakage-Enumeration Synonym Expansion
payload.description: When a question asks what things/items someone had broken or damaged and initial retrieval returns no direct 'broken' memory, use this to expand search terms before answering.
content: When a question asks what kinds of things a person had broken or damaged (e.g., 'what broke down', 'what was damaged', 'what things did X have broken'), do not conclude 'no information' after one literal search; supporting memories may use 'broke down', 'breakdown', 'accident', 'malfunction', 'issue', 'damaged', or 'repair'.

Run additional keyword or structured searches combining the person's name with breakage synonyms (broke, broken, broke down, breakdown, accident, malfunction, damage, issue, repair) and likely object categories (car, vehicle, bike, phone, appliance, device).
Check sufficiency after each search; continue until no new distinct broken/damaged items appear, and cite only memories that explicitly state an item was broken, damaged, or broke down.

candidates.solves: The Access agent answered 'no information' after a single literal search for 'broken' even though a memory stated Evan's new Prius 'broke down'. The reusable failure is premature no-info on enumerative damage questions when memory wording differs from query wording. This skill applies to future questions asking what things/items a person had broken, damaged, or had fail, requiring synonym expansion and sufficiency checks before concluding no evidence.

payload.name: Search intolerance and dietary restrictions for allergy questions
payload.description: When a question asks what someone is allergic to or cannot eat/drink due to allergies or intolerances, use broader retrieval: include preference/event memories and query terms like intolerant, cannot have, dairy-free, avoids, not only the word allergy.
content: During retrieval for allergy or dietary-restriction questions, include both 'preference' and 'event' memory kinds (or omit the memory_kind filter), and expand queries with intolerance/avoidance terms such as 'intolerant', 'cannot have', 'dairy-free', 'avoids'.

Treat memories that explicitly state intolerance or inability to consume a substance as direct evidence for an allergy or restriction answer, even if the word 'allergy' is absent and the memory is stored as a preference.

candidates.solves: Allergy queries that rely only on the literal word 'allergy' miss preference memories stating an intolerance or dietary avoidance (e.g., lactose intolerant, cannot have dairy). This Skill fixes that by requiring broader memory_kind coverage and intolerance/avoidance query expansions before answering. It applies to allergy or health-restriction questions, not ordinary taste/preference questions.

payload.name: Search event-achievement details for category-item lists
payload.description: When a question asks for specific items in a category a person engages with, and initial generic searches return only broad statements, run targeted searches pairing the person with the category and engagement/achievement terms (won, played), and inspect event/achievement memories before answering.
content: If a question asks for specific items in a category (e.g., video games, movies, books) a person engages with, do not answer from broad hobby or preference statements alone.

Run targeted searches pairing the subject with the category and engagement/achievement terms (e.g., '<person> played/won <category>', '<person> <category> tournament'), and inspect event and achievement memories for named items.
Only answer 'No information available' after such targeted event/achievement searches also fail to surface any named category items.

candidates.solves: Category-item list questions often retrieve only broad hobby/event statements while the named items are stored in event/achievement memories (e.g., winning a tournament 'playing Street Fighter'). The rule requires running targeted searches pairing the subject with the category and concrete engagement/achievement terms, and inspecting event/achievement memories before answering 'No information available'. Applies to any question asking for specific instances of a category a person engages with, not to questions answerable from broad preferences alone.

payload.name: Multi-angle retrieval for inspiration-source questions
payload.description: When a question asks what a person is inspired by, influenced by, or draws creative ideas from, use follow-up searches beyond literal 'inspired by' before answering.
content: When a question asks what someone is inspired by or where they get ideas, do not stop after a single hybrid search for 'inspired by' or 'inspiration'; relevant memories often do not contain those words.

Run at least one follow-up search using source descriptors and predicates such as validation/recognition, personal history or childhood stories, people they know, things they observe, imagination, creative process, and achievement events; include memory kinds profile, event, plan, and preference.
Before answering, judge sufficiency against all candidate source memories and do not finalize until either a broad set is collected or exhaustive multi-angle searches have been attempted.

candidates.solves: Questions asking what a person is inspired by often miss memories stored under varied source predicates rather than the literal word 'inspire'. Cause: stopping after one literal hybrid search. This Skill mandates multi-angle follow-up searches across source descriptors and memory kinds before answering. Applies to future inspiration/influence-source questions for any person, not to single-fact queries or answers already explicit in evidence.

payload.name: Count Created Works via Completion Events
payload.description: Use when a question asks how many creative works a person has written, created, completed, or produced.
content: When asked how many creative works a person has written/created/completed, search with creation and completion vocabulary: wrote/written/writing, created, completed, finished, just finished, plus artifact synonyms (screenplay/script/book/song/film/project) and ordinals (first, second, another).

Treat as distinct works any memories that name a separate artifact, including completion milestones and current writing plans; merge memories that refer to the same work from different angles before counting.
If the first search returns only submission, showing, or rejection events, run an additional search for completion milestone terms before finalizing the count.

candidates.solves: Failure caused by counting only submission/showing events and missing a distinct completion memory because queries used ownership vocabulary. Abstract rule: for 'how many X has Y written/created/completed', search creation/completion terms and artifact synonyms, include plan/completion memories naming distinct works, and merge same-work references before counting. Applies to counts of written/created works generally; not to ownership counts.

payload.name: Include plan memories when retrieving creative work inspiration
payload.description: When a question asks what inspired, motivated, or a creative work is about and includes a person or date, include plan and preference/profile memory kinds in retrieval; ongoing works are often stored as plans, not events.
content: When the user asks about the inspiration, motivation, or subject of a specific creative work (screenplay, book, film, project), do not restrict memory_kinds to event; include plan, preference, and profile, because ongoing or newly started works are often stored as plan memories.

If the question includes a date, run at least one search treating that date as the world_start/filter for plan memories, and combine it with the subject and creative-work terms; do not rely only on event-kind searches.

Before answering, require a retrieved memory that explicitly states the inspiration or subject; circumstantial memories such as favorite films or general writing enjoyment are not sufficient evidence.

candidates.solves: When a question asks what inspired or motivated a specific creative work (screenplay, book, film, project) at a date, the supporting memory is often a plan memory of an ongoing work, not an event. Restricting memory_kinds to event misses it, as happened when the agent searched only events and answered from a favorite film. Future inspiration/subject questions about current creative works should include plan memories and date-aligned retrieval; this does not apply to completed-work achievement retrieval already covered by creative-work skills.

payload.name: SearchAllWritingFormatsForEnumerationQuestions
payload.description: When a question asks what kinds or forms of writing or creative work someone produces (an enumeration, not only the current project), run searches with generic format terms and include completed or published works.
content: When a question asks what kinds or forms of writing a person produces (e.g., what do they write, what formats they work in), treat it as an enumeration of all their writing types, not just their current project.

Run at least one additional hybrid or keyword search using generic format terms such as 'writings', 'published', 'blog', 'essay', 'journal', 'story', 'book', 'script', or 'screenplay' rather than only 'currently working on' or project-specific phrases.
Include event memories describing completed works or works that received outside responses (performed, published, read by others), not only memories about current projects.

candidates.solves: Enumeration questions about a person's writing formats were answered from current-project searches, missing completed formats stored as events (e.g., a performed screenplay, a blog post read by others). The rule adds a second search using generic format terms and accepts completed-work events as evidence. Applies to future 'what kinds of writings/creative works does X produce' questions; not to questions explicitly about the current ongoing project.

payload.name: Expand-synonyms-when-counting-work-outcomes
payload.description: Use when a question asks how many times a person's work or creative output was rejected or received a repeated outcome, and memories may describe the work with different nouns.
content: When counting repeated outcomes for a person's work (e.g., how many times rejected, accepted, submitted), do not limit queries to the exact noun in the question; include synonyms and broader descriptions such as 'creative work', 'submission', 'project', or 'screenplay' when the question says 'scripts'.

Include derived noun forms of the outcome verb (e.g., 'rejection', 'decline') and phrases like 'another rejection', 'setback', or 'turned down' in keyword searches, not only verb inflections like 'rejected'.
After finding an initial matching event, run at least one additional search with the broader object terms before answering, and enumerate every distinct event memory that matches the asked outcome.

candidates.solves: The agent found only one rejection because its queries used only the literal noun 'scripts', missing a memory about 'another rejection ... for her creative work'. Counting repeated events requires synonym and broader-object searches anchored on the person, not just verb inflections from the question. Applies to future count questions about repeated outcomes for a person's work when memories phrase the object differently.

payload.name: IncludeCommunityWritingInCreativeWorkSearch
payload.description: When a question asks what kind of writing or creative work someone does, search for community participation (forum posts, comments, discussions, reviews) in addition to formal writing projects before answering.
content: When a question asks what kind of writing or creative content someone produces, do not limit queries to 'writing', 'articles', 'stories', or 'novel'; include community-writing terms such as 'forum', 'comments', 'discussion', 'posts', and 'reviews' in query expansions and keywords.

Treat memories about joining an online community, discussion group, or forum and sharing thoughts on favorite topics as potential evidence of that person's writing, even when the memory does not contain the word 'write' or 'writing'.

If the initial search returns only formal writing projects (e.g., articles, books), run at least one additional search targeting community participation before answering, so comments and reviews are not omitted.

candidates.solves: When a question asks broadly what kind of writing or creative work someone does, retrieval can miss community-writing activities (forum posts, comments, discussions, reviews) because queries target formal terms like 'articles' or 'novel'. This skill expands search vocabulary to text-producing community activities and accepts participation memories as writing evidence, ensuring complete answers; it is not needed when the question targets one specific formal work or genre.

payload.name: Include ongoing-profile memories for time-bound improvement questions
payload.description: When a question asks what someone did during a specific time period to improve or care for something (health, pets, skills), retrieve profile/relationship memories too, not just event memories in that date range.
content: If a question asks what <person> did in <month/period> to <improve/care for/manage> <subject>, do not restrict memory_kinds to 'event'; the supporting memory may be a 'profile' memory describing an ongoing membership, class, routine, or group participation that lacks an event date inside that period.

Run at least one search with memory_kinds including 'profile' (plus 'event' and, for planned actions, 'plan'), and do not require world_start to fall within the target month; ongoing profile facts remain valid evidence for actions taken during the period.

Before answering, if the event-only search returns activities but a profile memory explicitly states an action that matches the question (e.g., participates/joined/attends), prefer or include that memory as direct evidence rather than concluding with a list of related events.

candidates.solves: When a time-bounded 'what did X do to improve/care for Y' query retrieves only event memories near the dates, it can miss durable facts stored as profile memories (e.g., group membership, class enrollment). The failure is over-restriction to event kind and exact date window. Rule: for such queries, also retrieve profile memories and accept ongoing facts as evidence. Applies to future questions about actions, routines, or participation in a given period.
